topics.label: Introduction to cellular transformation and cancer genetics
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic frames the lecture, connects it to the practicals, and states its learning outcomes before the substantive material begins.

topics.label: Tumor virology and the discovery of cellular proto-oncogenes
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how tumor-virus research led from the idea of transmissible cancer to the discovery that transforming viruses capture normal cellular genes.

topics.label: Experimental assays of cellular transformation
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how researchers test whether genes and mutations can produce transformed cell properties and tumors.

topics.label: Functional classifications of cancer mutations
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic sets out the terms used to describe mutations by their effects on tumor formation and cellular maintenance.

topics.label: Mutation effects on growth-control pathways
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics show how mutations disrupt cell-cycle control and how the specific effect of a mutation, such as dominant-negative p53, shapes its consequences.

topics.label: Genetic instability caused by DNA repair defects
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how failures in DNA repair compromise genome integrity and produce sequence or chromosomal instability.

topics.label: Genetic instability from replication and mitotic errors
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics show how errors in copying or segregating the genome create instability and can promote tumor adaptation.

topics.label: Mutation timing in colorectal cancer progression
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic relates the timing and order of mutations, including chromosomal instability, to the progression of colorectal tumors.

topics.label: Hereditary cancer predisposition
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how inherited mutations in caretaker or gatekeeper genes raise cancer risk and illustrates that risk with hereditary cancer syndromes.

topics.label: BRCA2 restoration and the persistence of malignancy
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic uses BRCA2 restoration during treatment to show that a cancer can remain malignant even after its homologous-recombination function is restored.

topics.label: Lecture close: questions, further reading and next lecture
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic closes the lecture with an invitation for questions, a reading recommendation, and notice of the next lecture.
